title: Broken oaths
hook: he reproaches the emperor's officers who swore safe passage and broke it (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama's opening: a letter to an emperor that starts with God, not with grievance. Your line was begin with praise. Did a message of yours start with thanks? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

A promise is the cheapest thing in the world to make. It costs a breath. It is also one of the few things that can't be bought back once it's broken. Tradition tells it like this. Anandpur had been under siege for a long time. Food was gone. Word came from the emperor's side: leave the fort, and you will have safe passage. Oaths were sworn, tradition says, on what each side held holy. The Guru's household and his Sikhs went out into the night. And once they were out, the armies fell on them. The praise is finished now. In the next stretch of his letter, Guru Gobind Singh turns to the oath.
screen: `A PROMISE COSTS A BREATH.` → `LEAVE, AND YOU'LL BE SAFE.` → `ONCE OUTSIDE, THE ATTACK.`

segments.voice: The Zafarnama is written in Persian verse, and this part of it is plain speaking. Paraphrased, the Guru says: I had no trust in your oath. Your officers swore in God's name, and their words were false. A man who breaks his oath, he writes, cannot be trusted with anything. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't curse the emperor's faith. He holds the emperor to it. You call on God, he says, in effect; then keep the promises you make in God's name. The standard he reaches for is one the emperor already claims. That makes the letter harder to wave away, because it isn't an outsider's insult. It's a mirror. Then there's the weight of it. Some readers notice that the letter is written after terrible loss, and yet the charge is precise. Not you are evil, but you gave your word and broke it. A grievance that names one clear wrong can be answered. A grievance that names everything usually can't. And for Sikhs the oath runs the other way too. In the Gurus' teaching, truthful living stands above clever speech, and the Khalsa is asked to be someone whose word holds. The Zafarnama's anger at broken oaths is also a picture of the opposite: a person, or a people, who keep theirs. Look back over this week, too. Sparks from one fire. The wondrous drama. Only the servant. Through the battle at Bhangani. Head, not faith. Begin with praise. Read together, they sketch one person: a servant who praises first, names the cost, and stands behind his words.
screen: `I HAD NO TRUST IN YOUR OATH.` · `HE HOLDS THE EMPEROR TO HIS OWN FAITH.` · `ONE CLEAR WRONG, NAMED PRECISELY.` · `A PEOPLE WHOSE WORD HOLDS.` · then, large: `KEEP YOUR OATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your word today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one promise you've made that's still open. A call you said you'd return. A thing you said you'd fix. Something you told a child. Don't scold yourself about it. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a ticket you haven't used yet. Then picture the moment today when you keep it. Where you are, what you say, how it lands. If you pray, you can hold that promise before Waheguru as you breathe out. The bell holds the time.
Broken oaths. In the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh tells the emperor he had no trust in an oath sworn in God's name and then broken. Today's word.
Your line: keep your oath. Today, keep the promise you found in the sit, before the day ends, even if it's small. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and recite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to the emperor Aurangzeb, and its lines on broken oaths are often recalled in katha and in teaching about truthful living and keeping one's word.

fork.setup: you've been betrayed by people who swore an oath in God's name. you're writing to the man in charge of them. how do you make the charge?
options: hold them to the faith they already claim.
fork.reveal: Guru Gobind Singh holds the emperor to his own standard: a promise made in God's name should be kept. that makes it a mirror, not an insult.

original.note: Persian, the Zafarnama's language: an oath. the Guru writes that he had no trust in their oath.

trapdoor: what you thought: an angry letter about a battle.
what it means: a precise charge. you swore in God's name, and you broke your word.
what a scholar hears: the Guru argues from the emperor's own faith, which makes the letter a mirror rather than an outsider's insult.

notes: The Zafarnama verses on the oath are paraphrased, not quoted; please check the paraphrase ('I had no trust in your oath'; one who breaks his oath cannot be trusted) against the Persian.
